newsitem.title: FRANCE: Schneider to expand internally, acquire.
newsitem.headline: Schneider to expand internally, acquire.

text.p: French electrical distribution company Schneider, sitting on ample cash and borrowing capacity, wants to expand through organic growth and acquisitions, chairman Didier Pineau-Valenciennes said on Wednesday.

"We want to develop internally in all our activities. We have strategic developments, particularly in Asia...And in all these countries we will expand through organic growth and direct investment," he told a news conference.
He added, "We are also studying...possible acquisitions all over the world, on the North American continent, but also on the Asian continent."
Schneider was looking at small investments of the order of 100, 200 and 300 million francs but also much larger deals, he said.

The company was permanently studying opportunities to win world leadership in the sectors where it wanted to be and looking for market share, he said, adding that the company's cash and borrowing power gave it buying potential.
Schneider was open to partnerships in the high-voltage power business, where it had no chance of being a leader, and "conversations are going on with everyone", he said.

Schneider's net debt-equity ratio was down to 29 percent at the end of 1996, with shareholders equity of 18.88 billion and debt of 5.26 billion, compared to a ratio of 48 percent in 1995 and 136 percent in 1992, when it borrowed heavily to buy Square D and Telemecanique.

It will have little or no financial debt in the next couple of years, and will actually see an increase in equity capital as a 2.8 billion convertible bond is converted into shares and a three-billion TDI quasi-equity subordinated debt instrument is treated as capital, he said.
That gave it potential borrowing power of 20-25 billion francs and access to significant funds through rights issues.
The sale of non-core assets, such as Spie Batignolles, was essentially over but he did not rule out further disposals if the activity were not part of the core business.

Following the Spie sale, Schneider was now centred on its core electrical business, with 22.4 percent of 1996 sales from transmission and distribution, 31.4 percent from industrial control and automation, 22 percent from low-voltage power and 16.7 percent from final low voltage systems.
